blocks.prompt: Why a Train Can Pull So Much
blocks.text: A train can pull a very heavy load. One engine can pull a hundred cars full of rock. How? The answer is steel. The wheels are steel and the rails are steel. Both are hard and smooth. Hard, smooth things roll easily. A car tire squishes on the road, and squishing wastes energy. A steel wheel barely squishes at all. So the train rolls and rolls. But smooth has a cost. A train cannot stop fast. A long freight train needs more than a mile to stop. That is why we never play near the tracks.

because it squishes on the road
more than a mile

3.title: The Train That Steers Itself
3.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: The Engine That Broke Its Own Track
blocks.text: In 1804, a man named Richard Trevithick did something nobody had done before. He built a steam engine that could move itself. He put it on rails at an ironworks in Wales and it hauled ten tons of iron and seventy cheering men for almost ten miles. It worked. There was one problem. The engine was so heavy it cracked the iron rails underneath it. That is the story of early trains. The engine and the track had to grow up together. Twenty five years later, in 1829, a railway company held a contest to find the best locomotive. Engines lined up at a place called Rainhill. Some broke down. One was powered by a horse walking on a moving belt. It did not win. The winner was Rocket, built by George Stephenson and his son Robert. It reached about thirty miles an hour, faster than any horse could gallop for long. The next year the world's first real passenger railway opened between Liverpool and Manchester. People who had never traveled faster than a trotting horse suddenly could. Distance never felt the same again.

4.title: The Train That Steers Itself
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Train wheels are coned, not flat
Both wheels are locked to one axle
The cone steers the train around curves
The flange is only a backup
The side to side wobble is called hunting

blocks.prompt: The Wheel That Does the Thinking
blocks.text: Look closely at a train wheel and you will notice something odd. It has no steering wheel, no driver turning it, and yet a train takes a curve at speed without leaving the rails. Most people assume the flange does it. The flange is that lip on the inside edge of the wheel, and it does help, but it is a backup. It is the emergency fence, not the steering. The real trick is a shape. A train wheel is not flat where it touches the rail. It is slightly coned, wider near the inside and tapering outward, like a very shallow cup turned over. The two wheels on an axle are locked together, so they must spin at exactly the same speed. Now think about a curve. The wheelset drifts a little toward the outside of the bend. That shifts the outer wheel onto its fat part and the inner wheel onto its skinny part. In one turn, the fat part covers more ground than the skinny part. The outside travels farther, the inside travels less, and the whole wheelset swings gently into the curve. It steers itself. Even better, it self corrects. If the wheelset wanders off center on straight track, the cone pushes it back toward the middle without anyone touching a thing. The gentle side to side wobble it makes while correcting has a name. Engineers call it hunting. The wheel is a machine that solves a geometry problem thousands of times a minute, and it has no moving parts at all.

5.title: The Train That Steers Itself
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Steel on steel grips about ten times less than tire on road
A loaded freight train can need a mile to stop
A 2 percent slope is a mountain to a train
Westinghouse patented the air brake in 1869
Air pressure holds the brakes off, not on
Lose the air and every brake slams on

blocks.prompt: The Brake That Works by Failing
blocks.text: Everything wonderful about a train comes from one fact: steel on steel barely grips. A rubber tire on asphalt pushes back hard against a rolling car, which is why your bike coasts to a stop so quickly. A steel wheel on a steel rail pushes back roughly ten times less. That is why a single locomotive can drag a hundred loaded wagons across a continent while a truck of the same power struggles with one trailer. Now turn the fact over. The grip that will not slow you down also will not stop you. A loaded freight train traveling at fifty five miles an hour can need more than a mile of track to halt, even with every brake clamped down. The train is not being stubborn. There is simply not enough friction between wheel and rail to shed that much energy quickly. This is also why railway grades are so gentle. A hill a cyclist would call flat, say a two percent slope, is a serious mountain to a train. For decades the stopping problem was solved badly. Early trains used brakemen: men who rode on the cars and cranked handbrakes on, wagon by wagon, when the whistle sounded. It was slow, it was inconsistent, and it killed people. In 1869 George Westinghouse patented something better, and his second version, the automatic air brake, contained an idea worth understanding. A pipe of compressed air runs the length of the train. You might guess that air pressure applies the brakes. It does the opposite. Pressure holds the brakes off. Each car carries its own small reservoir of air and its own valve, and when the pressure in the pipe drops, every valve on every car dumps its reservoir into its brake cylinder and the brakes slam on. Think about what that means. If the train breaks in two, the pipe tears open, the pressure vanishes, and both halves stop themselves. If a hose leaks, the train stops. If the system fails, the train stops. Westinghouse designed a machine whose failure mode is safety. Engineers call this fail safe, and the principle now protects elevators, aircraft, and nuclear plants. It started on a railroad.

6.title: The Train That Steers Itself
6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Standard gauge is 4 feet 8.5 inches
Railway time began on the Great Western in 1840
Bristol clocks once carried two minute hands
November 18, 1883: the Day of Two Noons
Congress made standard time law in 1918
A French TGV hit 357 miles an hour in 2007

blocks.prompt: The Train That Rebuilt Time
blocks.text: Before the railway, noon was a local fact. It arrived when the sun stood highest over your particular patch of ground, and since the sun does not clear the horizon everywhere at once, every town kept its own slightly different clock. A town a dozen miles west of yours ran about a minute behind. Nobody minded. Nobody could travel fast enough to notice. The railway noticed immediately. A stagecoach took days to cross the gap between two clocks, so the discrepancy dissolved into the journey. A train crossed it before lunch. Suddenly a timetable had to answer an impossible question: when it says the train departs at 11:05, whose 11:05 does it mean? Worse, two trains sharing one track are only safe if both crews agree on what time it is. On a single track railway, a disagreement about the minute is a disagreement about which train is still coming. Britain solved it first, and solved it by force. The Great Western Railway ordered its stations onto London time in 1840, and other companies followed. For years this produced a peculiar sight: station clocks in Bristol carrying two minute hands, one for the town and one for the railway, ten minutes apart. People called the imported version railway time. It won. By 1855 nearly every public clock in Britain had surrendered to Greenwich, though the courts held out until 1880. America had the same problem across a far larger board. In the early 1880s, roughly fifty different railroad times were in use, and a traveler crossing the country reset a watch again and again. The railroads did not wait for Congress. They met, agreed among themselves, and on November 18, 1883, the railroads of the United States and Canada simply changed. Clocks were stopped or advanced to fit the new standard zones, four of them across the United States. In cities where the old local noon and the new railway noon fell apart, midday arrived twice. Newspapers called it the Day of Two Noons. Notice who did this. Not a government, not an astronomer, not a treaty. A private industry rewrote what time it was for a continent because its business could not function otherwise, and the public went along because the railroads printed the timetables everyone actually lived by. Congress did not make standard time federal law until 1918, thirty five years after the country was already using it. There is a pattern here worth keeping. A new technology rarely stays inside the problem it was built for. The steam locomotive was designed to move coal. It ended up moving noon.
